summary: Source decomposition of AN.4 from Tate's 1950 thesis (the admissible class Z, the Riemann-Roch/Lemma A mechanism, Main Theorem 4.4.1 with its two simple poles and the explicit class-number residue constant, the local functional equation with explicit archimedean gamma factors and p-adic root numbers, and the comparison identifying the adelic zeta integral with Hecke's L-function) together with Kedlaya's Chapter 22 for the distinction between Artin's induction theorem plus the provable continuation near Re(s) = 1 and the unproved Artin holomorphy conjecture. AN.1, AN.2 and AN.3 each receive one node decomposed from Kedlaya's notes: the completed zeta functional equation via theta inversion, the classical zero-free region with its full proof, and von Mangoldt's explicit formula with its truncation remainder and the resulting unconditional PNT error term. AN.0 and AN.5-AN.9 are not read. One scope problem in the existing atlas is recorded: the edge FF.1 -> AN.1 does not cover the composite-modulus Gauss sums that the Dirichlet L-function functional equation actually uses.

nodes.title: Continuation of zeta and the functional equation xi(s) = xi(1-s) from the theta inversion formula
nodes.statement: For Re(s) > 1 one has pi^{-s/2} Gamma(s/2) zeta(s) = integral_0^infty x^{s/2-1} omega(x) dx with omega(x) = sum_{n>=1} exp(-n^2 pi x), and splitting at x = 1 and using theta(x^{-1}) = x^{1/2} theta(x) gives pi^{-s/2} Gamma(s/2) zeta(s) = -1/(s(1-s)) + integral_1^infty (x^{s/2-1} + x^{(1-s)/2-1}) omega(x) dx. The right-hand side is meromorphic on all of C and invariant under s -> 1-s, so zeta extends meromorphically to C, xi(s) := (1/2) s(s-1) pi^{-s/2} Gamma(s/2) zeta(s) is entire and satisfies xi(1-s) = xi(s), equivalently zeta(1-s) = pi^{1/2-s} Gamma(s/2)/Gamma((1-s)/2) zeta(s). The zeros of zeta with Re(s) <= 0 are exactly the poles of Gamma(s/2) other than s = 0, i.e. the negative even integers (trivial zeros).
hypotheses: The interchange of sum and integral producing (5.1.2)-(5.1.3) is justified only for Re(s) > 1, by absolute convergence
The entirety of the right-hand side uses omega(x) = O(e^{-pi x}) as x -> +infty
The identification of the trivial zeros uses zeta(s) != 0 for Re(s) >= 1 (Kedlaya Theorem 1.5, Hadamard and de la Vallee-Poussin), which is a separate input

theta(x^{-1}) = x^{1/2} theta(x) holds for x > 0 and is deduced from Poisson summation for Schwartz functions (Theorem 5.6), applied to f(s) = e^{-pi x s^2} whose Fourier transform is x^{-1/2} e^{-pi s^2 / x}
proofSteps: Substituting t = pi n^2 x in Gamma gives (5.1.2) pi^{-s/2} Gamma(s/2) n^{-s} = integral_0^infty x^{s/2-1} e^{-n^2 pi x} dx for Re(s) > 0; summing over n for Re(s) > 1 gives the Mellin representation.

The theta inversion (5.1.3) gives omega(x^{-1}) = -1/2 + (1/2) x^{1/2} + x^{1/2} omega(x); substituting into the integral from 0 to 1 yields the two elementary poles 1/s and 1/(s-1) combined as -1/(s(1-s)).
Kedlaya proves (5.1.3) as Corollary 5.7 from Theorem 5.6 (Poisson summation for Schwartz f: sum_n f(n) = sum_n fhat(n)), with Lemma 5.5 supplying the needed decay of f and fhat.
Invariance of the right-hand side of (5.1.4) under s -> 1-s is immediate from its shape, and the poles at s = 0 and s = 1 are cancelled by the factor s(s-1) in xi.
acceptance: Check the two poles: zeta has a simple pole at s = 1 with residue 1, and pi^{-s/2}Gamma(s/2)zeta(s) has poles exactly at s = 0 and s = 1.
Check the trivial zeros come from Gamma(s/2), with s = 0 excluded by the factor s in xi.
Check that the derivation of (5.1.4) is only valid a priori for Re(s) > 1 and that the extension to Re(s) > 0 and then to C is by the analyticity of the integral, not by re-deriving the series.

sources.locator: Section 5.1, equations (5.1.2)-(5.1.5) and Remark 5.2, printed pp. 33-35
sources.excerpt: Hence for Re(s) > 1, pi^{-s/2} Gamma(s/2) zeta(s) = -1/(s(1-s)) + integral_1^infty (x^{s/2-1} + x^{(1-s)/2-1}) omega(x) dx. (5.1.4) ... One often writes this by defining xi(s) = (1/2) s(s-1) pi^{-s/2} Gamma(s/2) zeta(s), and then the functional equation is xi(1-s) = xi(s).
sources.match: Exactly the continuation formula, the definition of the completed function and the functional equation asserted in the node.

nodes.title: Functional equation for L(s,chi) with conductor, Gauss sum and parity, for primitive chi
nodes.statement: Let chi be a primitive Dirichlet character of level N. If chi(-1) = 1 (even), then with theta(x,chi) = sum_{n in Z} chi(n) exp(-n^2 pi x / N) one has pi^{-(1-s)/2} N^{(1-s)/2} Gamma((1-s)/2) L(1-s, chi-bar) = N^{1/2} c_{chi,1} pi^{-s} N^{s/2} Gamma(s/2) L(s,chi), where c_{chi,1} = tau(chi)/N and tau(chi) = sum_{l=1}^{N} chi(l) e^{2 pi i l / N}. If chi(-1) = -1 (odd), theta(x,chi) vanishes identically and one uses theta_1(x,chi) = sum_n n chi(n) exp(-n^2 pi x/N) instead, obtaining pi^{-(2-s)/2} N^{(2-s)/2} Gamma((2-s)/2) L(1-s, chi-bar) = -i tau(chi) N^{-1/2} pi^{-(1+s)/2} N^{(1+s)/2} Gamma((1+s)/2) L(s,chi). In both cases the functional equation relates two different L-functions unless chi = chi-bar.
hypotheses: chi PRIMITIVE of level N; primitivity is exactly what is needed for the uniform Fourier-coefficient identity c_{chi,m} = chi-bar(m) c_{chi,1} at m not coprime to N
N is an arbitrary modulus, in general composite; the Gauss sum tau(chi) is a sum over Z/N, not over the multiplicative group of a finite field
The even case uses theta(x,chi), the odd case theta_1(x,chi) and a different gamma factor and the extra factor -i; the two cases are not interchangeable
c_{chi,1} c_{chi-bar,1} = N^{-1} (equivalently |tau(chi)| = N^{1/2} for primitive chi) is quoted by Kedlaya as an exercise, not proved in the text read
proofSteps: For m coprime to N, c_{chi,m} = (1/N) sum_l chi(l) e^{-2 pi i l m/N} = chi-bar(m) c_{chi,1} by the substitution l -> lm; for m not coprime to N the same identity (6.1.3) needs primitivity and is left to the exercises.
This gives the theta transformation theta(x,chi) = (N/x)^{1/2} c_{chi,1} theta(x^{-1}, chi-bar).
Splitting the Mellin integral (6.1.1) at x = 1 and substituting x -> x^{-1} in one term gives the paired representation; using c_{chi,1} c_{chi-bar,1} = N^{-1} produces (6.1.4).
For odd chi the same scheme with theta_1 and the inversion formula (6.2.1) gives (6.2.2), with the shift of the gamma argument by 1 and the factor -i.
acceptance: Imprimitive test: for chi imprimitive induced by chi' of level N' | N, L(s,chi) differs from L(s,chi') by the finite Euler product over p | N, p not dividing N'; the functional equation above is stated only for primitive chi, so a consumer must record which Euler factors are missing.
Parity test: for chi odd the even-case formula is vacuous because theta(x,chi) = 0 identically; check that an implementation branches on chi(-1).
Conductor test: the powers N^{(1-s)/2}, N^{s/2} must be carried; dropping them breaks the equation.
Root-number test: |tau(chi)| = N^{1/2} for primitive chi; check this separately, since the text read leaves it as an exercise.

sources.locator: Sections 6.1-6.2, (6.1.3), (6.1.4), the definition of tau(chi), and (6.2.2), printed pp. 39-41
sources.excerpt: For m not coprime to N, we must assume chi is primitive, and then again c_{chi,m} = chi-bar(m) c_{chi,1} (6.1.3) but this is not so obvious; see exercises. ... tau(chi) = N c_{chi,1} = sum_{l=1}^{N} chi(l) e^{2 pi i l / N} ... pi^{-(2-s)/2} N^{(2-s)/2} Gamma((2-s)/2) L(1-s,chi-bar) = -i tau(chi) N^{-1/2} pi^{-(1+s)/2} N^{(1+s)/2} Gamma((1+s)/2) L(s,chi). (6.2.2)
sources.match: Gives the primitivity hypothesis, the Gauss sum with its modulus-N definition, and both the even and odd functional equations with their distinct gamma factors and the factor -i.

nodes.title: The classical zero-free region Re(s) >= 1 - c/log Im(s) for zeta
nodes.statement: There exists c > 0 such that zeta has no zero in {s : Re(s) >= 1 - c/log Im(s), Im(s) >= 1}.
hypotheses: Uses the Hadamard product representation of xi ((8.2.5) in the source), obtained from Lemma 8.3 (xi has order <= 1) and Theorem 8.7 (Hadamard factorization for entire functions of order <= 1)
The estimate (8.3.4) is valid for 1 <= Re(s) <= 2 and |Im(s)| >= 1, where the Gamma and constant terms are dominated by a constant times log|Im(s)|
Positivity of Re(1/(s-rho)) and Re(1/rho) for the discarded terms uses Re(rho) > 0 and Re(s - rho) > 0, i.e. it uses that all nontrivial zeros lie in the critical strip
The constant c is ineffective in the form stated here only to the extent that the implied constants are unspecified; the argument itself is explicit
proofSteps: From 3 + 4 cos(theta) + cos(2 theta) >= 0 and the Dirichlet-series expansion of -Re(zeta'/zeta), obtain (8.3.1): -3 Re(zeta'(sigma)/zeta(sigma)) - 4 Re(zeta'(sigma+it)/zeta(sigma+it)) - Re(zeta'(sigma+2it)/zeta(sigma+2it)) >= 0 for sigma > 1 and t real.
Bound the sigma term by the simple pole at s = 1: -zeta'(sigma)/zeta(sigma) < 1/(sigma-1) + O(1) ((8.3.2)).
Bound the sigma + 2it term using the logarithmic derivative of the Hadamard product (8.3.3) and discarding the positive sum over zeros: -Re(zeta'(s)/zeta(s)) < O(log|Im(s)|) ((8.3.5)).
Bound the sigma + it term by keeping only the summand of the zero rho = beta + it: -Re(zeta'(s)/zeta(s)) < O(log|t|) - 1/(sigma - beta) ((8.3.6)).
Combining gives 4/(sigma - beta) < 3/(sigma-1) + O(log|t|); choosing sigma = 1 + c'/log|t| yields beta < 1 - c/log|t|.
acceptance: Boundary test: the argument also reproves nonvanishing on Re(s) = 1, since a zero at 1 + it would force the left side of the 3-4-1 inequality to tend to -infinity as sigma -> 1+ (using 4 > 3 and that zeta(sigma + 2it) does not diverge).
Check that the region excludes Im(s) < 1; the statement as proved says nothing near the real axis, where the separate Remark 7.4 numerical argument is used.
Check that discarding the sum over zeros is only legitimate in one direction (it gives an upper bound for -Re(zeta'/zeta)).

sources.locator: Theorem 8.8 and its proof, (8.3.1)-(8.3.6), printed pp. 50-51
sources.excerpt: Theorem 8.8 There exists a constant c > 0 such that there is no zero of zeta in the region {s in C : Re(s) >= 1 - c/log Im(s), Im(s) >= 1}. ... Combining (8.3.1) with (8.3.2), (8.3.5) (taking s = sigma + 2it), and (8.3.6) (taking s = sigma + it), we obtain 4/(sigma - beta) < 3/(sigma - 1) + * log|t|. For sigma = 1 + */(log|t|), this yields beta < 1 - */log|t| as desired.
sources.match: Statement and complete proof as summarized in the node's steps, with the exact combination of the three bounds.

nodes.title: von Mangoldt's explicit formula with truncation remainder, and the resulting PNT error term
nodes.statement: For x >= 2 and T > 0, psi(x) - x = - sum_{rho : |Im(rho)| < T} x^rho/rho - zeta'(0)/zeta(0) - (1/2) log(1 - x^{-2}) + R(x,T) with R(x,T) = O( x log^2(xT)/T + (log x) min(1, x/(T <x>)) ), where rho runs over the zeros of zeta in the critical strip Re(s) in [0,1] and <x> denotes the distance from x to the nearest prime power other than possibly x itself. Combining this with a zero-free region Re(rho) < 1 - f(|Im rho|) and a zero count N(T) = O(T log T) gives |psi(x) - x| = O(x exp(-c sqrt(log x))) for some c > 0.
hypotheses: x >= 2 and T > 0; the remainder degrades as x approaches a prime power, which is what the min(1, x/(T<x>)) factor records
The term -(1/2) log(1 - x^{-2}) is exactly -sum over the TRIVIAL zeros of x^rho/rho, so the trivial zeros are not omitted but summed in closed form
The final error bound uses the zero-free region of Theorem 7.5/8.8 (f(T) = c/log T) and Hadamard's count N(T) = O(T log T) (Theorem 7.6)
Kedlaya defers the proof of the explicit formula to his Theorem 9.9, of the zero-free region to Theorem 8.8, and of the zero count to Remark 8.6
proofSteps: Given a zero-free region beta < 1 - f(|gamma|), bound |x^rho| = x^beta < x^{1 - f(T)} for |gamma| < T, giving (7.2.1) |sum_{|gamma|<T} x^rho/rho| <= x^{1-f(T)} sum_{|gamma|<T} 1/gamma.
Convert the sum over zeros into a Stieltjes integral against the counting function: (7.2.2) sum_{0<|gamma|<T} 1/gamma = N(T)/T + integral_0^T t^{-2} N(t) dt.
With N(T) = O(T log T) this gives sum_{|gamma|<T} 1/gamma = O(log^2 T), hence sum x^rho/rho = O(x^{1-f(T)} log^2 T).
Substituting into the explicit formula gives |psi(x) - x| = O( x log^2(xT)/T + x (log^2 T) exp(-c (log x)/(log T)) ); balancing the two terms with T = exp(sqrt(log x)) gives the stated bound.
acceptance: Check that the contour-shift bookkeeping is complete: the pole of zeta at s = 1 gives the main term x, the trivial zeros give -(1/2)log(1-x^{-2}), and the value zeta'(0)/zeta(0) is a constant term; none of these may be dropped.
Check that no GRH-type hypothesis is used: the result is unconditional, but the constant c is inherited from an unspecified constant in the zero-free region.
Check the T -> infinity limit: for fixed x, R(x,T) = o(1), giving the unrestricted (conditionally convergent) explicit formula; the source explicitly warns that this form is less useful.
Prime-power test: at x equal to a prime power the remainder's <x> factor must be interpreted with the 'other than possibly x itself' convention.

sources.locator: Theorem 7.2 with its remainder, Definition 7.3, (7.2.1)-(7.2.2), Theorems 7.5-7.7, printed pp. 43-45
sources.excerpt: Theorem 7.2 von Mangoldt's formula. For x >= 2 and T > 0, psi(x) - x = - sum_{rho:|Im(rho)|<T} x^rho/rho - zeta'(0)/zeta(0) - (1/2) log(1 - x^{-2}) + R(x,T) ... R(x,T) = O( x log^2(xT)/T + (log x) min(1, x/(T<x>)) ). ... Theorem 7.7 Error bound in the prime number theorem. For some c > 0, |psi(x) - x| = O(x exp(-c sqrt(log x))).
sources.match: Gives the explicit formula with its exact truncation remainder and the derived unconditional error bound, together with the two inputs (zero-free region and zero count) used in the derivation.

nodes.title: The class Z of admissible functions on the adeles and the zeta integral zeta(f,c)
nodes.statement: Let k be a number field, V its ring of valuation vectors (adeles) and I its idele group. Let Z be the class of complex-valued functions f on V satisfying: (Z1) f and f-hat are continuous and in L_1(V); (Z2) for every idele u and vector y, both sum_{xi in k} f(u(y+xi)) and sum_{xi in k} f-hat(u(y+xi)) converge, uniformly in the pair (u,y) for y in V and u in any fixed compact subset of I; (Z3) f(u)|u|^sigma and f-hat(u)|u|^sigma are in L_1(I) for sigma > 1. For f in Z and a quasi-character c of the idele class group of exponent greater than 1, define zeta(f,c) = integral_I f(u) c(u) d*u.
hypotheses: Quasi-characters are taken trivial on k^* (i.e. they are idele class quasi-characters); the exponent of c is the real number sigma with |c(u)| = |u|^sigma
(Z2) is precisely the hypothesis that makes the Riemann-Roch/Poisson step legitimate, and (Z3) is what makes the defining integral converge for exponent > 1
The topology on I is the idele topology, which is strictly stronger than the subspace topology from V; the source flags this explicitly
proofSteps: Tate defines Z by the three conditions Z1-Z3 (thesis p. (4.15)) and observes that Z1 and Z2 are exactly what is needed for the Riemann-Roch theorem to apply to functions of Z, while Z2 in addition permits the definition of zeta-functions.
Definition 4.4.1 then attaches zeta(f,c) to each f in Z, defined for all quasi-characters of exponent greater than 1.
The parametrization of an equivalence class of quasi-characters as c(u) = c_0(u)|u|^s with s uniquely determined makes each class a Riemann surface, exactly as in the local theory of section 2.4.
acceptance: Check that a function in Z is not merely Schwartz-Bruhat by fiat: Z1-Z3 are conditions on f AND on f-hat, and the verification for the specific f built in section 4.5 occupies a separate argument (thesis p. (4.24)).
Check the exponent convention: 'exponent greater than 1' corresponds to Re(s) > 1 when c(u) = |u|^s.
Check that quasi-characters are required to be trivial on k^*, so that they descend to the idele class group.

sources.locator: Conditions Z1-Z3 and Definition 4.4.1, thesis p. (4.15) = scan p. 49
sources.excerpt: We let Z denote the class of all functions f(y) satisfying the three conditions: Z1) f(y) and f-hat(y) are continuous, in L_1(V) ... Z2) sum_{xi in k} f(u(y+xi)) and sum_{xi in k} f-hat(u(y+xi)) are both convergent for each idele u and vector y, the convergence being uniform in the pair (u,y) for y ranging over V and u ranging over any fixed compact subset of I. Z3) f(u)|u|^sigma and f-hat(u)|u|^sigma in L_1(I) for sigma > 1. ... Definition 4.4.1: We associate with each f in Z a function zeta(f,c) of quasi-characters, defined for all quasi-characters c of exponent greater than 1 by zeta(f,c) = integral f(u) c(u) d*u.
sources.match: Verbatim the three admissibility conditions and the definition of the global zeta integral used throughout the rest of the packet.

nodes.title: Adelic Poisson summation (Riemann-Roch) and the t -> 1/t functional equation for the truncated integral
nodes.statement: (Riemann-Roch, Theorem 4.2.1) For f satisfying the stated hypotheses, sum_{xi in k} f(xi t b) = (1/|t b|) sum_{xi in k} f-hat(xi/(t b)). (Lemma A) For all quasi-characters c, zeta_t(f,c) + f(0) integral_E c(t b) d*b = zeta_{1/t}(f-hat, c-hat) + f-hat(0) integral_E c-hat((1/t) b) d*b, where zeta_t(f,c) = integral_J f(tb) c(tb) d*b, E is a fundamental domain for J mod k^*, and c-hat(u) = |u| c^{-1}(u). (Lemma B) integral_E c(tb) d*b equals kappa t^s if c(u) = |u|^s, and 0 if c is non-trivial on J.
hypotheses: k^* is discrete and cocompact of covolume 1 in the norm-one idele group J (the product formula |alpha| = 1 for alpha in k^*, Theorem 4.3.1 of the thesis)
The decomposition I = T x J with a chosen splitting T, and the normalization d*u = d*b dt/t, are fixed before the computation
Lemma A's proof uses hypothesis Z2 to interchange the sum over k^* with the integral over the relatively compact set E
Lemma B's dichotomy is the statement that the integral over J mod k^* of a character of that group is the total measure kappa or 0 according as the character is trivial or not
proofSteps: Write zeta_t(f,c) + f(0) integral_E c(tb) d*b as a sum over alpha in k^* of integrals over alpha E, using that J is the disjoint union of the alpha E.
Change variables using d*(alpha b) = d*b and c(alpha t b) = c(t b) (c is trivial on k^*), turning the expression into integral_E [ sum_{xi in k} f(xi t b) ] c(tb) d*b.
Apply Riemann-Roch (Theorem 4.2.1) to replace sum_{xi in k} f(xi t b) by (1/|tb|) sum_{xi in k} f-hat(xi/(tb)).
Substitute b -> 1/b (with d*b invariant) to recognize the result as zeta_{1/t}(f-hat, c-hat) + f-hat(0) integral_E c-hat((1/t) b) d*b; reversing the steps completes the proof.

Lemma B: integral_E c(tb) d*b = c(t) integral_E c(b) d*b, and the latter is the integral over J mod k^* of the character represented by c, hence kappa (the measure of E) or 0; in the trivial case c(t) = |t|^s = t^s.
acceptance: Check the interchange in step 1 is justified only under Z2, and only for b in the relatively compact E.
Check the two extra terms f(0) and f-hat(0): they are exactly the boundary contributions that become the two simple poles of the continued zeta-function.
Check that Lemma B's constant kappa is the measure of the multiplicative fundamental domain, and is the same constant as in the residue formula of the main theorem.

sources.locator: Lemma A and Lemma B with proofs, thesis pp. (4.16)-(4.17) = scan pp. 50-51
sources.excerpt: Lemma A: For all quasi-characters we have zeta_t(f,c) + f(0) integral_E c(tb) d*b = zeta_{1/t}(f-hat, c-hat) + f-hat(0) integral_E c-hat((1/t)b) d*b. ... (Riemann-Roch theorem 4.2.1) ... Lemma B: integral_E c(tb) d*b = kappa t^s if c(u) = |u|^s, 0 if c(u) is non-trivial on J.
sources.match: Gives both lemmas with the exact role of Riemann-Roch (Theorem 4.2.1) inside the proof of Lemma A, as recorded in the proof steps.

nodes.title: Main Theorem 4.4.1: continuation, simple poles with residues -kappa f(0) and +kappa f-hat(0), and zeta(f,c) = zeta(f-hat, c-hat)
nodes.statement: Every zeta-function zeta(f,c) extends by analytic continuation to the domain of all quasi-characters. The extended function is single-valued and regular except at c(u) = 1 and c(u) = |u|, where it has simple poles with residues -kappa f(0) and +kappa f-hat(0) respectively, where kappa = 2^{r_1} (2 pi)^{r_2} h R / (w sqrt(|d|)) is the volume of the multiplicative fundamental domain. It satisfies the functional equation zeta(f,c) = zeta(f-hat, c-hat) with c-hat(u) = |u| c^{-1}(u).
hypotheses: f in Z; c an idele class quasi-character (trivial on k^*)

r_1, r_2 are the numbers of real and complex places, h the class number, R the regulator, w the number of roots of unity and d the discriminant of k; this is the analytic class number formula constant
The double-bracket terms in the continuation formula occur ONLY when c is trivial on J, in which case one writes c(u) = |u|^s and needs Re(s) > 1 for the auxiliary integrals to converge
The integrals from 1 to infinity converge for all c because they are over the region |u| >= 1
proofSteps: For c of exponent > 1 write zeta(f,c) = integral_0^infty zeta_t(f,c) dt/t and split at t = 1.

The integral from 1 to infinity converges for all c: it equals the integral of f(u)c(u)d*u over the half of I where |u| >= 1, which converges the better the smaller the exponent of c, and converges for exponent > 1, hence for all c.

Use Lemma A and Lemma B to transform the integral from 0 to 1 into an integral from 1 to infinity of zeta_t(f-hat, c-hat), producing the correction terms { kappa f-hat(0)/(s-1) - kappa f(0)/s } when c is trivial on J.

The resulting expression zeta(f,c) = integral_1^infty zeta_t(f,c) dt/t + integral_1^infty zeta_t(f-hat,c-hat) dt/t + { kappa f-hat(0)/(s-1) - kappa f(0)/s } is analytic in c, giving the continuation and exhibiting the poles and residues.
For c(u) = |u|^s one has c-hat(u) = |u|^{1-s}, so the whole expression is unchanged under (f,c) -> (f-hat, c-hat); hence the functional equation.
acceptance: Residue check: at c = 1 (s = 0) the residue is -kappa f(0); at c = |u| (s = 1) it is +kappa f-hat(0). An implementation that reports only one pole is wrong.
Constant check: kappa = 2^{r_1}(2 pi)^{r_2} h R/(w sqrt|d|) is the classical analytic class-number constant; check it against the Dedekind zeta residue after the section 4.5 comparison.
Check that the double-bracket terms are present only for c trivial on J; for a ramified class of quasi-characters the continued function is entire.
Check that c-hat(u) = |u| c^{-1}(u) matches the local definition used in section 2.4.

sources.excerpt: Main Theorem 4.4.1: (Analytic Continuation and Functional Equation of the zeta-Functions). By analytic continuation we may extend the definition of any zeta-function zeta(f,c) to the domain of all quasi-characters. The extended function is single valued and regular, except at c(u) = 1 and c(u) = |u| where it has simple poles with residues -kappa f(0) and +kappa f-hat(0), respectively (kappa = 2^{r_1}(2 pi)^{r_2} h R/(w sqrt|d|) = volume of the multiplicative fundamental domain). zeta(f,c) satisfies the functional equation zeta(f,c) = zeta(f-hat, c-hat), where c-hat(u) = |u| c^{-1}(u) as in the local theory.
sources.match: Verbatim statement including the explicit residue constant that is the analytic class-number formula constant required by AN.4's acceptance condition.

nodes.title: Local functional equation zeta(f,c) = rho(c) zeta(f-hat, c-hat), with explicit archimedean gamma factors and p-adic root numbers
nodes.statement: For a local field k there is a factor rho(c), depending only on the quasi-character c and not on f, with zeta(f,c) = rho(c) zeta(f-hat, c-hat) for all admissible f, valid in the strip 0 < exponent(c) < 1 where both sides are defined. One has rho(c-hat) = c(-1)/rho(c) and rho(c-bar) = c(-1) conj(rho(c)) (Lemma 2.4.3), hence |rho(c)| = 1 when the exponent of c is 1/2 (Corollary 2.4.1). Explicitly: for k = R, zeta(f, |.|^s) = pi^{-s/2} Gamma(s/2) and zeta(f_pm, pm|.|^s) = pi^{-(s+1)/2} Gamma((s+1)/2), giving rho(|.|^s) = 2^{1-s} pi^{-s} cos(s pi/2) Gamma(s) and rho(pm|.|^s) = -i 2^{1-s} pi^{-s} sin(s pi/2) Gamma(s); for k = C the classes are represented by c_n(r e^{i theta}) = e^{i n theta}; for k p-adic, rho(|.|^s) = N(d)^{s-1/2} (1 - N(p)^{s-1})/(1 - N(p)^{-s}) with d the different, and for c ramified of conductor f with c(pi) = 1, rho(c|.|^s) = N(d f)^{s-1/2} rho_0(c) where rho_0(c) = N(f)^{-1/2} sum_{epsilon} c(epsilon) e^{2 pi i Lambda(epsilon / pi^{ord(d f)})} is a root number of absolute value 1, the sum being over representatives of the cosets of 1 + f in the units.
hypotheses: The factor rho depends only on the equivalence class of c, i.e. on c_0 and s; the independence of f is the content of the local main theorem
|rho(c)| = 1 holds exactly on the line exponent(c) = 1/2, and is deduced from the two identities of Lemma 2.4.3, not assumed
In the p-adic ramified formula the normalization is c(pi) = 1 for the chosen uniformizer, and the argument of the additive character involves the different d as well as the conductor f
The archimedean measures are the ones fixed in section 2.2 (for k = C, |alpha| = r^2 is the SQUARE of the ordinary absolute value and d(xi) is twice ordinary Lebesgue measure)
proofSteps: Tate obtains the functional equation from the identity zeta(f,c) zeta(f-hat_C, c-hat) = zeta(f-hat, c-hat) zeta(f_C, c) for an auxiliary f_C in the overlapping strip, which shows the ratio zeta(f,c)/zeta(f-hat, c-hat) is independent of f.

Lemma 2.4.3 (1): zeta(f,c) = rho(c) zeta(f-hat, c-hat) = rho(c) rho(c-hat) zeta(f-hat-hat, c-hat-hat) = c(-1) zeta(f,c) using f-hat-hat(alpha) = f(-alpha) and c-hat-hat = c; hence rho(c) rho(c-hat) = c(-1).
Lemma 2.4.3 (2) is the corresponding computation with complex conjugates.
Corollary 2.4.1: on exponent 1/2 one has c-bar = c-hat, so equating the two expressions for rho gives rho(c) conj(rho(c)) = 1.

Section 2.5 computes rho on each equivalence class by evaluating zeta(f_C, c) for an explicitly chosen f_C: Gaussians in the archimedean cases, and in the p-adic ramified case the characteristic function of a suitable coset, whose Fourier transform is N(d)^{-1/2} N(p)^n times the characteristic function of 1 + p^n.
acceptance: Gamma-factor check: the even real class gives pi^{-s/2}Gamma(s/2) and the odd real class pi^{-(s+1)/2}Gamma((s+1)/2); these must match the archimedean factors used in the classical completed L-function of AN.1.

Root-number check: |rho_0(c)| = 1 is proved from Corollary 2.4.1; independently, rho_0(c) is a normalized Gauss sum of the residue-field character, so its modulus can be cross-checked against the finite-field Gauss sum modulus q^{1/2} (see the note in this packet's gaps: the two facts are proved by different routes and neither is imported here).
Different/conductor check: the exponent of N(d f) is s - 1/2, so dropping either the different or the conductor changes the functional equation.
Complex-case check: the normalization |alpha| = r^2 must be carried, or the complex gamma factor comes out wrong.

Lemma 2.4.3: 1.) rho(c-hat) = c(-1)/rho(c). 2.) rho(c-bar) = c(-1) conj(rho(c)). ... Corollary 2.4.1: |rho(c)| = 1 for c of exponent 1/2.

nodes.title: Identification of the adelic zeta-function with Hecke's L-function, and the global functional equation for zeta(s,chi)
nodes.statement: Fix a finite set S of places containing all archimedean ones, and let c = prod_p c_p be an idele class character unramified outside S, written for p in S as c_p(u_p) = c_p-tilde(u_p-tilde) |u_p|_p^{i t_p}. For p not in S the local zeta-function of the standard f_p is zeta_p(f_p, c_p |.|^s) = N(d_p)^{-1/2}/(1 - chi(p) N(p)^{-s}), where chi is the associated ideal character. Defining the classical Hecke zeta-function zeta(s,chi) = prod_{p not in S} (1 - chi(p) N(p)^{-s})^{-1} for Re(s) > 1, one has zeta(f, c|.|^s) = prod_{p in S} zeta_p(f_p, c_p|.|^s) . prod_{p not in S} N(d_p)^{-1/2} . zeta(s,chi), equivalently zeta(s,chi) = sum over integral ideals a prime to S of chi(a) N(a)^{-s}. Combining with the global and local functional equations gives zeta(1-s, chi^{-1}) = prod_{p in S} rho_p(c_p-tilde |.|^{s + i t_p}) . prod_{p not in S} chi(d_p)^{-1} N(d_p)^{s - 1/2} . zeta(s,chi). These ideal characters chi are exactly Hecke's characters and this is the functional equation Hecke proved.
hypotheses: S finite containing all archimedean places; c unramified outside S, equivalently c = prod c_p with c_p unramified for p not in S and prod_p c_p(alpha) = 1 for alpha in k^*
The Euler product for zeta(s,chi) runs only over p NOT in S: the Euler factors at the ramified places are not included in zeta(s,chi) and appear instead as the local factors zeta_p for p in S
The product decomposition zeta(f,c) = prod_p zeta_p(f_p, c_p) requires Theorem 3.3.1 on restricted direct products and holds for quasi-characters of exponent greater than 1
The factors N(d_p)^{-1/2} come from the different and are part of the normalization, not a cosmetic constant
proofSteps: For p not in S the local integral is a geometric series: zeta_p(f_p, c_p|.|^s) = sum_{v >= 0} chi(p^v) N(p)^{-vs} N(d_p)^{-1/2} = N(d_p)^{-1/2}/(1 - chi(p)N(p)^{-s}), because c_p(u_p) = chi(p^{ord_p u_p}).
Multiplying over all p and using Theorem 3.3.1 gives the displayed factorization of zeta(f, c|.|^s).

Tate notes the alternative route: expanding I into cosets of I_S and integrating over each coset directly gives the additive expression zeta(s,chi) = sum over integral ideals prime to S of chi(a)/N(a)^s.
Treating f-hat in the same way gives zeta(f-hat, c-hat |.|^s-hat) = prod_{p in S} zeta_p(f-hat_p, ...) . prod_{p not in S} chi(d_p) N(d_p)^{-s} . zeta(1-s, chi^{-1}) for Re(s) < 0.

Equating the two expressions via the global functional equation zeta(f,c) = zeta(f-hat, c-hat) and dividing by the local factors, each of which satisfies its own local functional equation with factor rho_p, yields the displayed functional equation for zeta(s,chi).
acceptance: Ramified Euler factor check: zeta(s,chi) as defined omits the primes in S. A consumer that claims a completed L-function must reinstate those factors via the local zeta_p, and must record which they are.

Different check: the factors N(d_p)^{-1/2} on the left and chi(d_p)^{-1}N(d_p)^{s-1/2} on the right must be tracked; for k = Q the different is trivial and they disappear, which is why the classical statement looks simpler.
Chebotarev/Frobenius convention check: chi(p) is the value of the ideal character at the prime p, matching c_p(u_p) = chi(p^{ord_p u_p}); an inverse convention flips the functional equation.
Test k = Q, S = {infinity}: zeta(s,chi) becomes the Riemann zeta function and the functional equation reduces to the classical one with the archimedean rho computed in section 2.5.

sources.locator: Section 4.5, Euler-product computation and definition of zeta(s,chi), thesis p. (4.23) = scan p. 57
sources.excerpt: zeta_p(f_p, c_p|.|^s) = integral c_p(u_p)|u_p|^s d*u_p = sum_{v=0}^infty chi(p^v) N(p)^{-vs} . N(d_p)^{-1/2} = N(d_p)^{-1/2}/(1 - chi(p)N(p)^{-s}) ... If therefore we introduce the classical zeta-function zeta(s,chi), defined for Re(s) > 1 by the Euler product zeta(s,chi) = prod_{p not in S} 1/(1 - chi(p)N(p)^{-s}), we can write zeta(f, c|.|^s) = prod_{p in S} zeta_p(f_p, c_p|.|^s) . prod_{p not in S} N(d_p)^{-1/2} . zeta(s,chi).

sources.excerpt: Our functional equations zeta(f-hat, c-hat) = zeta(f,c) and zeta_p(f_p,c_p) = rho_p(c_p) zeta_p(f-hat_p, c-hat_p) yield for zeta(s,chi) the functional equation zeta(1-s, chi^{-1}) = prod_{p in S} rho_p(c_p-tilde|.|^{s+i t_p}) . prod_{p not in S} chi(d_p)^{-1} N(d_p)^{s-1/2} . zeta(s,chi). ... These ideal characters chi, which we have constructed out of idele characters, are exactly the characters which Hecke introduced in order to define his 'new type of zeta-function'.

nodes.title: Artin L-functions: meromorphic continuation by induction and the m-th root trick, versus the unproved holomorphy conjecture
nodes.statement: Let K/Q be finite Galois with G = Gal(K/Q) and rho : G -> GL_n(C) with character chi. The incomplete Artin L-function is L(rho,s) = prod_p det(1 - rho(Frob_p) p^{-s})^{-1}, the product taken over unramified p only. Then (Artin's induction theorem) every character of G is a Q-linear combination of characters induced from cyclic subgroups; and (the provable weakening of Artin's conjecture) for every rho, L(rho,s) extends to a meromorphic function on a neighbourhood of Re(s) >= 1, is non-vanishing on Re(s) = 1 for s != 1, and has at s = 1 a pole of order equal to the multiplicity of the trivial representation in rho. Consequently (Chebotarev) for any conjugacy class C of G the set of primes p with Frob_p in C has natural density #C/#G. Artin's conjecture, that L(rho,s) is meromorphic on all of C with no poles away from s = 1 and with pole order at s = 1 equal to that multiplicity, remains a conjecture.
hypotheses: K/Q finite Galois; Frob_p is defined up to conjugacy only for unramified p (Lemma 22.1), which is why the product is taken over unramified p
The Euler product converges absolutely for Re(s) > 1, uniformly on Re(s) >= 1 + epsilon, and does not vanish there

The abelian base case of the continuation theorem requires class field theory: one must write the one-dimensional sigma of an abelian subgroup H as a ray class character; the source defers this to its reference [14]

The passage from rho^{oplus m} to rho uses that L(rho,s)^m is holomorphic and non-vanishing in a neighbourhood of Re(s) >= 1 after removing trivial subrepresentations, so an m-th root can be chosen there; this argument gives NOTHING outside that neighbourhood, which is exactly why it does not prove Artin's conjecture
The Euler factors at ramified primes are omitted here; the source states that the correct definition uses the determinant of rho on the inertia invariants but does not carry it out
proofSteps: Theorem 22.3 (Artin): by orthogonality of characters it suffices, for each conjugacy class, to construct a linear combination of induced characters non-vanishing only on that class; take g in the class generating a cyclic H, take a combination of one-dimensional characters of H supported at g, and induce.

Theorem 22.4 (sketch in the source): prove the claim first for rho = Ind_H^G sigma with H abelian and sigma one-dimensional, using class field theory; by Theorem 22.3 deduce the claim for rho^{oplus m} for a suitable m; then take the m-th root on a neighbourhood of Re(s) = 1 after reducing to rho with no trivial subrepresentation.

Theorem 22.5 (Chebotarev): imitate the proof of Dirichlet's theorem, using the pole orders at s = 1 of the L(rho,s) as rho runs over irreducible characters of G, together with the orthogonality relations, to extract the density #C/#G.

The source records that the induction argument gives only meromorphy in a neighbourhood of Re(s) >= 1; full meromorphy on C with the asserted pole structure is Conjecture 22.2, known for rho trivial, for dim rho = 1 (Kronecker-Weber plus Dirichlet L-functions), for rho induced from a one-dimensional representation, and for odd two-dimensional rho with solvable image (Langlands-Tunnell) or with image A_5 (via Serre's conjecture).
acceptance: Scope check: the theorem actually proved is meromorphy NEAR the line Re(s) = 1, not on all of C; a consumer that uses holomorphic continuation of an Artin L-function to the whole plane is using a conjecture.
Ramified-factor check: the L-function as defined here omits the ramified Euler factors, so any comparison with a Hecke L-function via class field theory must reinstate them (inertia invariants).
Rationality check: Theorem 22.3 gives a Q-linear, not Z-linear, combination; this is why one passes to rho^{oplus m} and needs the m-th root step.
Density check: Chebotarev with C = {1} recovers the density 1/#G of totally split primes; with G abelian it recovers Dirichlet's theorem.

(Sketch of proof) One first proves the claim for rho = Ind_H^G sigma for any abelian subgroup H of G and any one-dimensional representation sigma: H -> GL_1(C). This requires class field theory in general, because one has to first write sigma as a ray class character. See [14]. ... Theorem 22.5 Chebotaryov. gaps.title: Atlas edge FiniteFieldsAndCharacterSums:FF.1 -> AnalyticNumberTheory:AN.1 is under-scoped for composite moduli
gaps.detail: AN.1 requires FF.1 in the current atlas. What AN.1 actually needs (Kedlaya section 6.1, printed p. 40) is the Gauss sum tau(chi) = sum_{l=1}^{N} chi(l) e^{2 pi i l/N} of a PRIMITIVE Dirichlet character of an arbitrary level N, together with the identity c_{chi,m} = chi-bar(m) c_{chi,1} for all m (valid at m not coprime to N only for primitive chi) and |tau(chi)| = N^{1/2}. FF.1's stated scope (checked in data/atlas.json) is 'additive and multiplicative characters, orthogonality, Gauss and Jacobi sums' of a FINITE FIELD, built on FF.0 which constructs finite fields; for composite N the group (Z/N)^* is not the unit group of a finite field and Z/N is not a field. The finite-ring material is FF.4's declared scope ('Galois rings, additive polynomials ...'), but FF.4 sits after FF.2 and FF.3 in the FF chain, so routing AN.1 through FF.4 would introduce a long and probably unintended dependency. Recommendation (raised in HANDOFF.md, not applied here): either widen FF.1 to characters of finite abelian groups / Z/N with its own Gauss sums, or give AN.1 its own Dirichlet-character node. Nothing in this packet assumes either resolution.

gaps.detail: Verified: Kedlaya's Theorem 22.4 is presented as a sketch whose first step (the case rho = Ind_H^G sigma with H abelian and sigma one-dimensional) 'requires class field theory in general, because one has to first write sigma as a ray class character', with a reference to his [14]. Next source action: read the class field theory statement (Artin reciprocity for ray class groups) in Kedlaya's own class field theory notes, https://kskedlaya.org/papers/cft-ptx.pdf, and check whether ClassFieldTheory stages in the atlas already own it.

gaps.title: Root number rho_0(c) versus the finite-field Gauss sum modulus: relation noted, dependency NOT claimed
gaps.detail: Tate's ramified local factor contains rho_0(c) = N(f)^{-1/2} sum_epsilon c(epsilon) e^{2 pi i Lambda(epsilon/pi^{ord(d f)})}, which is literally a normalized Gauss sum of a character of the residue field when the conductor exponent is 1. The EXT-08 FiniteFieldsAndCharacterSums packet decomposes |tau(chi,psi)| = q^{1/2} (SGA 4 1/2 [Sommes trig.] Remarque 4.4). These are the same numerical fact in the tame case, but Tate proves |rho_0(c)| = 1 from Corollary 2.4.1, i.e. from the local functional-equation formalism, NOT from a Gauss-sum computation, and his formula covers arbitrary conductor exponent. No prerequisite edge FF.1 -> AN.4 is therefore proposed: this is a cross-check, not a dependency. Recorded here so that a later reviewer does not add the edge on the strength of shared vocabulary.

gaps.title: Tate's residue constant versus the analytic class number formula
gaps.detail: Verified: Main Theorem 4.4.1 states the residues as -kappa f(0) and +kappa f-hat(0) with kappa = 2^{r_1}(2 pi)^{r_2} h R/(w sqrt|d|), described as the volume of the multiplicative fundamental domain. Not verified: the computation of that volume (Tate sections 4.1-4.3), nor the derivation of the classical statement 'the Dedekind zeta function of k has a simple pole at s = 1 with residue 2^{r_1}(2 pi)^{r_2} h R/(w sqrt|d|)' from it, which requires choosing the specific f of section 4.5 and dividing out the local factors. Next source action: read Tate section 4.3 (scan pp. 44-48) and complete the specialization.
